[00:00 - 00:02] A high-pitched, sustained electronic tone plays.
[00:02 - 00:05] A male voice asks, "Why don't I see Nirvana right now?"
[00:05 - 00:07] Silence.
[00:07 - 00:13] A different, slightly synthetic-sounding male voice replies, "You do not see Nirvana right now because you imagine a seer and a world, and neither is there."
[00:13 - 00:15] Silence.
[00:15 - 00:23] A third male voice, sounding like a lecture recording with an Indian accent, begins: "What is called manyana is the imagining in egoistic terms, imparting reality to illusory things."
[00:24 - 00:31] The same voice continues, "Only looking is there, nothing worth looking at. Only seeing is there, nothing to be seen."
[00:33 - 00:43] The voice continues, "The law of dependent arising is already implicated. There is therefore no seer apart from the phenomenon of seeing, according to the Tathagata."
[00:46 - 00:52] The voice continues, "Samsara is a whirlpool as far as ordinary beings caught up in it are concerned."
[00:52 - 00:59] The voice continues, "Now what about the arahants? How is the idea of this whirlpool presented in the case of the arahants?"
[00:59 - 01:09] The voice continues, "It is simply said that for them there is no whirling round, for there to be a designation. Vattang tesam natthi pannyapanaya."
[01:09 - 01:15] The voice continues, "So in their case, there is no whirling round to justify a designation."
[01:15 - 01:19] The voice continues, "This then is something deeper than the whirlpool itself."
[01:19 - 01:26] The voice continues, "The whirlpool can be pointed out because of its activity, but not so easily the emancipated ones."
[01:26 - 01:31] The voice continues, "And that is why there is so much controversy regarding the nature of the Tathagata."
[01:31 - 01:40] The voice continues, "The image of the whirlpool in its relation to the emancipated ones is beautifully presented in the following verse from the Chulavagga of the Udana."
[01:40 - 01:52] The voice recites Pali text: "Acchichi vattang vyagha nirasan, visukka saritana sandati. Chinnang vattang na vattati, esepan to dukk..." The speech cuts off abruptly mid-word.
[01:52 - 02:01] Silence for approximately 9 seconds.
[02:01 - 02:05] The voice resumes, "In this context too, the term attasambhuta is mentioned."
[02:05 - 02:22] The voice continues, "When we reflect deeply on the significance of this term, we are first of all reminded of the vortex simile we employed to explain the reciprocal relationship between consciousness and name

s3.text:
[00:00 - 00:02] A high-pitched sine wave tone plays.
[00:02 - 00:04] A male voice asks, "What keeps it going?"
[00:04 - 00:07] Silence.
[00:07 - 00:18] The same male voice continues, "Thirst keeps it going. Impelled by that making it into something, it runs towards the mirage. The gap is ignored. What impels one to ignore that gap is thirst."
[00:18 - 00:19] Silence.
[00:19 - 00:24] A different male voice speaks, "Perception. What impels one to ignore that gap is craving."
[00:24 - 00:28] Silence with faint background noise.
[00:28 - 00:37] The second voice continues, "Because of this misconception the world is in a tangle. Names and concepts, particularly the nouns, perpetuate the ignorance in the world."
[00:37 - 00:38] A bird chirps.
[00:38 - 00:48] The second voice continues, "Therefore insight is the only path of release. And that is why a meditator practically comes down to the level of a child in order to understand name and form."
[00:48 - 00:58] The second voice continues, "He may even have to pretend to be a patient in slowing down his movements for the sake of developing mindfulness and full awareness."
[00:58 - 01:00] Silence with bird chirping.
[01:00 - 01:06] The second voice continues, "So we see that there is something really deep in nama-rupa, even if we render it as name and form."
[01:06 - 01:07] A throat clearing sound.
[01:07 - 01:11] Silence.
[01:11 - 01:22] The second voice continues, "There's an implicit connection with name as conventionally so called, but unfortunately this connection is ignored in the commentaries when they bring in the idea of bending to explain the word name."
[01:22 - 01:24] Silence.
[01:24 - 01:33] The second voice continues, "So we need not hesitate to render nama-rupa by name and form. Simple as it may appear, it goes deeper than the worldly concepts of name and form."
[01:33 - 01:34] Bird chirp.
[01:34 - 01:51] The second voice continues, "Now if we are to summarize all what we have said in this connection, we may say, name in name and form is a formal name. It is an apparent name. Form in name and form is a nominal form. It is a form only in name."
[01:51 - 02:02] Long silence.
[02:02 - 02:12] The second voice continues, "In this way we can understand the difference between the two words papañca and pamāṇa in respect of the nuances associated with them."
[02:12 - 02:20] The second voice continues, "Commentaries very often explain the term papañca simply as a synonym of craving,

[00:00 - 00:02] Silence followed by a faint click.
[00:02 - 00:13] A male voice speaks: "He does not delight in Nibbana. Why so? Because he knows that delighting is the root of suffering, and from becoming comes birth, and to the one become there is decay and death."
[00:13 - 00:20] Silence. A thumping sound occurs around 00:16.
[00:20 - 00:29] The same voice resumes: "It seems then that the Tathagata does not delight in Nibbana, because delighting is the root of suffering."
[00:29 - 00:35] The voice continues: "Now, nandhi is a form of grasping, upadana, impelled by craving."
[00:35 - 00:39] Silence. A throat clearing is audible.
[00:39 - 00:50] The voice continues: "It is sometimes expressly called an upadana. Ya vedanasu nandi tad upadanam. Whatever delighting there is in feeling, that is a grasping."
[00:50 - 01:03] The voice continues: "When there is delighting, there is grasping. When there is grasping, there is bhava, becoming or existence. From becoming comes birth, and to the one who has thus come to be, there is decay and death."
[01:03 - 01:10] Silence.
[01:10 - 01:29] A different male voice begins: "All that is known to the Tathagata. It is precisely because of this full understanding that he has not taken his stand upon it. He has no stance in regard to all that. This is the gist of the first paragraph of the discourse, which sounds more or less a paradox."
[01:29 - 01:41] The second voice continues: "It is because of this apparently queer state of affairs that the Tathagata has to confess that it would be a falsehood on his part to say all that I do not know."
[01:41 - 01:54] The second voice continues: "If someone asks whether it is because he does not know that he takes no stance, he cannot say yes. As a matter of fact, it is precisely because he has understood that he takes no stance."
[01:54 - 02:02] The second voice continues: "But the worldlings are of the opinion that knowledge of a thing entitles one to assert it dogmatically."
[02:02 - 02:14] The second voice continues: "To say I both know it and know it not, or I neither know it nor am ignorant of it, would also be mistaken by the world as a prevarication or equivocation."
[02:14 - 02:19] The second voice continues: "The first paragraph of the discourse has to be understood in this light."
[02:19 - 02:40] The second voice continues: "The commentary has it that the earth shook at five points in the discourse. According to it, the three significant terms janami, abhannasin, and viditam, I know, I have fully understood, and all that is known to the Tathagata, represent the plane of omniscience, sabbannuta bhumi, peculiar to a Buddha."

This is the gist of what Venerable Punnamantani Putta is trying to put across through this discourse. This shows that the conceit 'am' arises due to the five grasping groups."
00:49 - 00:53: Silence.
00:53 - 01:30: The human voice continues, "The gist of this paragraph is that the non-manifestative consciousness, which is infinite and all-lustrous, is free from the qualities associated with any of the concepts in the list, such as the earthiness of earth and the wateriness of water. That is to say, it is not under their influence, it does not partake of them, ananubhutam. Whatever nature the world attributes to these concepts, whatever reality they invest it with, that is not registered in this non-manifestative consciousness. That is why this consciousness is said to be uninfluenced..."

01:50 - 01:51: Silence.
01:51 - 02:13: The human voice continues, "It says that the Buddha, the kinsman of the sun, has compared form to a mass of foam, feeling to a water bubble, perception to a mirage, preparations to a banana trunk, and consciousness to a magic show. These five similes bring out the insubstantiality of the five grasping groups. Thus..."
02:13 - 02:17: Silence.

00:00 - 00:02: A high-pitched sine wave tone plays.
00:02 - 00:04: A female voice asks, "How is Nirvana attained?"
00:04 - 00:07: Silence.
00:07 - 00:25: A male voice speaks clearly without background noise: "Nirvana is only attained now, in seeing just the seeing with no 'I' added. Then it will not carry you, nothing to stand on, nowhere to land, neither here nor there nor in between. This itself is the end of suffering."
00:25 - 00:26: Brief pause.
00:26 - 00:48: A different male voice, recorded with audible bird chirping in the background, speaks: "And when to you, Bahiya, there will be in the seen just the seen, in the heard just the heard, in the sensed just the sensed, in the cognized just the cognized. Then, Bahiya, you are not by it. And when you are not by it, you are not in it. And when, Bahiya, you are not in it, then, Bahiya, you are neither here nor there nor in between. This itself is the end of suffering."
00:48 - 00:54: Silence lasting six seconds, with bird chirping audible.
00:54 - 01:18: The same male voice continues: "The basic principle in this training seems to be the discipline to stop short at bare awareness. Diṭhe diṭṭhamattaṁ, sute sutamattaṁ, etc. The latter half of the discourse seems to indicate what happens when one goes through that training. The entire discourse is a presentation of the triple training of morality, concentration, and wisdom in a nutshell."
01:18 - 01:22: Silence with bird chirping.
01:22 - 01:35: The voice says, "As for a simile, let us take up the razor, which is such a useful requisite in our meditative life. There's a certain special way in sharpening a razor."
01:35 - 01:36: A click or edit sound occurs. The voice says, "Comment."
01:36 - 02:10: The voice speaks in an explanatory tone: "I just wanted to explain to those who might not be familiar with it. This is... the Venerable is speaking about the type of razor used in old times and which is still accustomed to be used in the forest tradition, which is like like like a long blade and then a handle. And so one has to sharpen it on a stone in order to be able to to to shave one's head, which as monastics we have to do very regularly. End of comment."
02:10 - 02:12: Silence.
02:12 - 03:36: The voice resumes the main text: "There's a certain special way in sharpening a razor. With the idea of sharpening the razor, if one grabs it tightly and rubs it on the sharpening stone, it will only become blunt. Parāmasanā, grasping, grabbing, is something like that. What then is the alternative? A more refined and softer approach is required, as meant by the term samāsanā. There's a proper mode of doing it. 00:00 - 00:07: A male voice speaks, "He creates a picture out of it. He imagines something picturesque in it."
00:07 - 00:09: A brief pause with a faint click or pop sound.
00:09 - 00:36: The voice continues, "In fact, the allusion is not to the artist's mind but to the spectator's mind. It is on account of the three defilements of lust, hate, and delusion nurtured in his mind for a long time that he is able to appreciate and enjoy that picture. Such is the nature of those influxes. That is why the Buddha declared that this mind is far more picturesque than the picture in question."
00:36 - 00:41: Silence lasting approximately 5 seconds.
00:41 - 01:59: The voice resumes, "In the Satipatthana Sutta we find the following instruction in regard to the keeping of postures. Yatha yathava panassa kayo panihito hoti tatha tathanam pajanati. In whatever way his body is disposed, so he understands it. This is suggestive of the attempt of a spectator to understand the mimicry of an actor or an actress in a pantomime. While attending to one's postures, one feels as if one is watching a one-man dumb show. One gets an opportunity to watch it even more keenly when one comes to the section on full awareness, sampajanya kabbha, dealing with the minor postures, khuddaka iriyapatha. The worldlings are in the habit of creating material objects in accordance with the factors on the name side in a very, in an extremely subtle manner. By grasping the four elements under the influence of personality view, sakkaya ditthi. The material objects around us are recognized as such by grasping the four elements. The definition of the form aspect in name and form points to such a conclusion."
01:59 - 02:07: Silence lasting approximately 8 seconds.
02:07 - 03:06: The voice speaks Pali text followed by English translation, "Uppasampajja vihareyyam, yad ariya itarai ayatana upasampajja viharanti ti. Iti anuttare su vimokkhe su api ayam upata apayato uppajjati piyapajjheta domanassam. Yam eva rupam domanassangidam mocari ne kamasi tam domanassam. When by knowing the impermanence, change, fading away, and cessation of forms, one sees as it actually is with right wisdom that forms both formerly and now are all impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. One arouses a longing for the supreme deliverances thus: When shall I enter upon and abide in that sphere that the noble ones now enter upon and abide in? In one who arouses such a longing for the supreme deliverances, unhappiness arises conditioned by that longing. Such unhappiness as this is called unhappiness based on renunciation."
03:06 - 03:10: A short pause.
03:10 - 03:54: The voice continues, "Possessed by it. If we grasp something, we are caught by it. This is the moral behind the parable of the gem.
